notes.text: Sear the fillets in batches, two or three at a time, and keep the first batch warm on a plate under foil.

move.title: Crisp skin, tender fish
move.body: Trout is a thin, mild fish with skin that turns as crisp as a chip when it's seared. Today you'll dry the fillets well, lay them skin side down in shimmering oil, press them flat, and wait for the skin to release on its own. Most of the cooking happens on the skin side. Then a quick turn, a little butter and lemon, and a check at 145°F.

callback.body: In pineapple teriyaki salmon, you left the fish alone until it browned and slid when nudged. Skin works the same way, only more so: it sticks hard at first, then lets go by itself once it's crisp.

why.title: Dry skin crisps
why.body: Wet skin steams and turns rubbery. Patted dry with paper towels, and dried again just before it goes in the pan, it browns and crisps instead.

why.title: Press it flat
why.body: Fish skin shrinks the moment it hits hot oil, and the fillet curls up off the pan. Pressing it gently with the spatula for the first 15 seconds keeps the whole skin touching the pan, so it crisps evenly.

why.title: Wait for it to let go
why.body: Raw skin sticks to the pan. As it browns and crisps, it loosens and lets go on its own. Pull too soon and it tears; wait and it slides.

why.title: Mostly on the skin side
why.body: The skin protects the thin flesh from the heat. Cooking most of the way skin side down crisps the skin while the flesh cooks gently from below. You'll see it turn from see-through to solid, working up the side.

why.title: Fan on, window open
why.body: A hot pan and fish skin make smoke and a strong smell. Turn the stove fan on high before you start, and open a window if you can.

why.title: 145°F, and it flakes
why.body: Trout is thin, so it's done quickly. The thermometer slid into the side of the thickest part should read 145°F, and the flesh should flake when pressed with a fork.

wrong.fix: It was turned too soon, or the pan wasn't hot enough. Next time, wait for the shimmer, and give it another minute before you try again.
Press it flat with the spatula right away. Next time, press for the first 15 seconds.

wrong.sign: The skin is soft, not crisp
wrong.fix: It was wet, or the pan was crowded. Dry it well, and cook in batches with space between fillets.
The oil was too hot. Turn the heat down a little, and keep the fan on high.

quiz.q: Why press the fillet with the spatula at the start?
choices: So the shrinking skin stays flat on the pan

quiz.q: How do you know the skin is ready to turn?
choices: It lets go of the pan on its own

quiz.q: What does trout need to reach?

substitutions.note: Tilapia has no skin. Sear the darker side, where the skin was, first, the same way; it won't crisp, but it will brown.

steps.text: Turn the stove fan on high, and open a window if you can.
Cut the lemon in half: juice one half into the small bowl and cut the other into wedges. Chop the parsley.
Lay the trout on the plate, skin side up. Pat both sides very dry with paper towels, then sprinkle the salt and pepper on both sides.
steps.tip: Run your fingertips along each fillet for pin bones, as in week 21, and pull any you find.

steps.text: Throw the paper towels and the fish's package away, and wash your hands with soap.
Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
steps.look: The oil ripples like a heat haze, but isn't smoking.

steps.text: Pat the skin dry once more. Lay each fillet in the pan skin side down, laying it away from you. Press each one flat with the spatula for 15 seconds.
steps.tip: Leave space between the fillets. Cook in batches if they don't fit.

steps.text: Put the raw-fish plate in the sink and wash your hands.
Leave the fillets alone, without moving them, until the skin is deep golden and lets go of the pan, and the flesh has turned solid most of the way up the sides.
steps.look: The fish is solid about three-quarters of the way up, and a fillet slides when you nudge it.

steps.text: Turn the heat down to medium. Gently turn each fillet with the spatula, turning it away from you. Add the butter to the pan.
As the butter melts and foams, tip the pan a little and spoon the butter over the fish a few times.
Slide the thermometer into the side of the thickest fillet. It needs to read at least 145°F, and flake when you press it with a fork. If not, cook 30 seconds more and check again.

Turn off the stove. Move the fillets to plates skin side up, so the skin stays crisp. Pour the lemon juice into the butter left in the pan, swirl it, and spoon it around the fish, not over the skin. Scatter the parsley on top and serve with the lemon wedges.
steps.tip: The handle stays hot for a long time. Leave an oven mitt on it so nobody grabs it bare-handed.
